annotationRationale: The approved visible editorial note confirms uniform one-to-one assignments, resolving the stem's implicit assignment model. The problem tests favorable-outcome counting in a uniform permutation model. The alternatives explain the central no-repeat count through loop structure and inclusion-exclusion, respectively. For audit context, allowing students to receive independent uniform tutor assignments with tutor sharing would instead give \(\binom{6}{2}(1/6)^2(5/6)^4=3125/15552\), which is unlisted. That different model is excluded by the editorial clarification; the original stem, choices, key and grading remain unchanged.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is correct. No area repair is needed.

review.questionCheck: The supplied publication note makes the assignments uniformly random bijections. Under that clarification, the favorable count is 15·9=135 out of 720, giving B, 3/16. The stem alone does not explicitly prohibit tutor sharing; independent assignments would instead give 3125/15552, which is unlisted. The editorial note resolves this ambiguity explicitly. No figures or grading-status contradictions are present.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: The two retained methods provide useful, accessible alternatives for the four-student count: classifying loops and correcting overlapping repeat conditions. The reference's 3×3 slot argument offers another calculation of the same small count but adds insufficient benefit to require a third method.
review.annotationCheck: Assessing cnm_h137 and supporting it with cnm_h239 and cnm_h234 matches the uniform probability model, selection of the repeating pair, and permutation counts. The additional concepts are appropriately attached to their individual methods. No contextual annotation is needed.
review.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is correct. No area repair is needed.

methodReviews.mathCheck: Fixing Monday is valid because relabeling its tutors gives the same Tuesday count for every Monday assignment. There are 6!=720 Tuesday bijections and 15 choices of the repeating pair. A permutation of the other four without repeats has loop lengths 2+2 or 4, giving respectively 3 pairings and 3!=6 directed loops. These cases are exhaustive and disjoint, so the probability is 15(3+6)/720=3/16.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Both cited references support the repeating-pair and four-person derangement reduction. Neither supplied reference presents this loop classification; it is an independently justified extension in original prose. The source-informed-original designation correctly distinguishes these third-party references from official MAA material.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The tutor labels explain why Monday can be fixed. Following moves explains the closed loops, excludes one-student loops, and makes both case counts reconstructible. Fixing A removes starting-point duplication without incorrectly identifying opposite loop directions.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: All four immediate nodes are used: classical probability, unordered pair selection, factorial permutation counts, and combined addition and multiplication. The elementary loop argument is fully derived and needs no separate catalog entry.

methodReviews.mathCheck: For a chosen repeating pair, forcing k of the remaining four students to repeat leaves (4-k)! assignments. Thus inclusion-exclusion gives 24-4·6+6·2-4·1+1=9. The triple intersections correctly include the all-four-repeat assignment; its total weight is 1-4+6-4+1=0. Selecting the unique repeating pair gives 15·9 favorable assignments, hence 3/16.

The inclusion-exclusion derivation is a project-authored extension, supported conceptually by the supplied mapping rather than attributed to either source. The source-informed-original basis and prose are appropriate.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The first move identifies the overlapping unwanted conditions. Each table entry follows from choosing forced repeats and permuting the remaining students, and the accompanying explanation justifies the alternating corrections. The method independently establishes the denominator and avoids double counting the repeating pair.
